input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Our first screening is planned for March 21 in the old science auditorium. The society has used that room for years, but the projection booth is being renovated, so we have to use the portable screen and the digital projector from the media lab. The event is open to students and staff, and we have not decided whether to reserve seats for alumni. The room holds about 140 people, and the fire marshal asked us to keep both side aisles clear. We should put that information on the event page before tickets go live.

Mara Chen is coordinating the program, and she has proposed a small series about cities at night. The first film is a silent short from 1927. The second is a documentary made by a local student group, and the third is still under discussion. We received permission for the documentary, but not yet for the silent film, so we cannot publish the full list until the rights office confirms the screening license. Mara said, “I would rather announce two films accurately than advertise three and have to pull one.” That seems sensible, and the poster draft should say the third title will be announced later rather than imply that the selection is final.

We met on Tuesday in the student union and discussed the event schedule. The doors should open at 6:30, and the introduction should begin at 7:00. The program is expected to run for about two hours, including a short break after the documentary. We also talked about asking a faculty member to introduce the silent film. Professor Elena Rao has tentatively agreed, but she needs the final running time before she confirms her arrival. The break matters because the projector needs to cool down for a few minutes and because volunteers will be handing out a one-page guide. If the film license arrives after the printing deadline, we should still hold the screening but remove the silent film and extend the introduction to include a short discussion instead.

For publicity, we have three things to finish. First, update the society website with the date, room access details, and the note about the pending third title. Second, send the campus events office a short description and an image they can use in their weekly email. Third, make a square graphic for the society account and a version that works on the library screens. The current draft uses a photograph from a student archive, and we have permission to display it on campus, but we do not yet have permission for the society’s public social media page. So please do not post that version online until we hear back from the photographer. Jules said, “The image is beautiful, but the caption has to identify the photographer and the archive.” We should include that credit wherever the image appears.

Number one: the ticket form should ask whether a guest needs step-free access. Number two: it should offer a way to request captions for the documentary. And number three: it should make clear that admission is free but registration is requested because the auditorium has limited capacity. We have not chosen whether to close registration at 120 or leave it open and manage the line at the door. Mara will check with the room coordinator on Friday. If we get no answer by then, keep the form open and put a note on the event page that walk-ins are welcome while space remains. Do not promise a seat to anyone who has not registered, because the fire marshal’s limit applies to everybody in the room.

The volunteers have different jobs, and we should give them a clear arrival time. Nina and Caleb are checking the projector and testing the subtitles at 5:30. Two society members will set up the welcome table and the sign-in sheets, and one volunteer will stay near the main entrance to direct guests to the accessible route. The old side entrance is shorter, but it has two steps, so it cannot be the route listed on the event page. We should also bring a small lamp for the table, since the overhead lights near the screen will be dimmed before the screening starts. I wrote down that we need tape, extension cords, water cups, and the printed guides. I nearly wrote paper plates there, but we do not need those.

Our spending estimate is modest. The media lab will lend us the projector and screen at no charge, and the student union has offered the auditorium without a rental fee. We still need to pay for printing and possibly for the screening license. The printing estimate is eighty-four dollars for 150 guides. The rights office has not given us a fee yet, so leave that line blank in the budget rather than guessing. We can use up to $200 from the society’s events fund without a separate vote, but if the license costs more than that, we have to ask the members at the next meeting. The treasurer wants receipts for every purchase, including small items, and would like the final expense list within a week of the event.

We should meet again on Monday at 4:00 in the media lab, unless Mara hears from the rights office that afternoon. In that case, she will send a message, and we can decide by email whether the announcement needs to change. I can bring the revised poster and a printed copy of the running order. Caleb will bring the subtitle test file, and Nina said she can ask the library about using its screens. I am not asking anyone to confirm the third film before we have written permission, and I do not want the public announcement to suggest that Professor Rao has confirmed until she has the final running time. The remaining points for Monday are the registration limit, the image credit, and whether we need a backup laptop.

The goal is to make the evening welcoming without making promises we cannot keep. The society can explain the program clearly and still say that one title is pending. We should give guests useful access information before they arrive and leave enough time for the volunteers to test the equipment. The film license and the caption request both affect what we can publish, so we need to check those details before sending the final announcement. If the license comes through in time, we can add the silent film title and keep the planned running order. If it does not, we will use the approved documentary and the discussion in its place. The date and venue stay the same either way, and our next update should report only what has been confirmed."}]
